panels.title: Islamic foundation
panels.text: Islam forbids magic (sihr) and condemns those who learn it to harm others (al-Baqarah 2:102); the witches here are Shakespeare's fiction, written for a king who feared witchcraft. Islam also warns against seeking power for its own sake: the Prophet ﷺ advised a Companion not to ask for leadership (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

panels.title: Introduction: 'How does Shakespeare present ambition in Macbeth?'
points: Context: written about 1606 for James I, soon after the Gunpowder Plot
Thesis: ambition becomes deadly when it silences conscience
Roadmap: first in the prophecies, then in the murder, finally in the tyranny

Answer: Written for James I soon after the Gunpowder Plot, Macbeth explores the terror of treason. Shakespeare presents ambition as a force that becomes deadly once it silences conscience. This is seen first in Macbeth's response to the prophecies, then in Duncan's murder and finally in his tyranny.

panels.title: How does Macbeth respond to the prophecies?
points: Embed 1: Macbeth is shaken by a 'horrid image'
Embed 2: he hopes 'chance may crown' him
Embed 3: but soon hides his 'black and deep desires'
Analyse the change across the three

Answer: At first Macbeth is shaken by a 'horrid image' and hopes 'chance may crown' him without action; yet within one scene he is hiding his 'black and deep desires', which shows how quickly temptation becomes intention.

panels.title: Why does Shakespeare make Lady Macbeth attack Macbeth's manhood?
points: What happens: she taunts him: 'then you were a man'
Writer's choice: Shakespeare makes her redefine manhood as violence
Intention: to explore how false ideas of strength lead to evil
Audience response: a Jacobean audience is disturbed by the reversed roles
Answer: Shakespeare uses Lady Macbeth's taunt, 'then you were a man', to explore how a false idea of manhood can drive a man to murder, disturbing an audience who expected loyalty and order.

panels.title: How does Shakespeare present Macbeth's guilt after the murder?
points: Long sentence: build the evidence of the ocean image and lost sleep
Medium sentence: analyse what it shows
Short sentence: land the judgement

Answer: Staring at his hands, unable to say 'Amen' and certain that 'all great Neptune's ocean' could not clean them, Macbeth is overwhelmed by what he has done. His guilt is immediate and total. Nothing can wash it away.
